newsitem.title: USA: Rocket for Saturn probe springs leaks.
newsitem.headline: Rocket for Saturn probe springs leaks.

text.p: A giant U.S. Air Force rocket that was to launch NASA's multibillion-dollar Cassini probe toward Saturn began leaking during a launch pad test this week, NASA officials said on Thursday.

The 20-story Titan 4B rocket, which was to launch the $3.4 billion mission on Oct. 6, leaked supercold liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen during a fuelling test on Tuesday, space agency spokesman Bruce Buckingham said.
"There is a possibility of a launch delay," he said. "We are assessing the nature of the problem."
Engineers were trying to determine the cause of the leaks and a fresh fuelling test was to be performed to check for further problems.

The Titan 4B, the most powerful unmanned U.S. rocket, was to launch the mission from Cape Canaveral during a narrow launch window that runs from Oct. 6 to Nov. 4 so the probe could arrive at Saturn in July 2004.
A launch in November or December would delay the probe's arrival by 5 to 26 months and would use more manoeuvring fuel, shortening the lifetime of the probe.

The Cassini mission has generated controversy because of its nuclear power source. Protesters have claimed a launch pad explosion could release plutonium. NASA says the chances of a radioactive release are one in 900.
Project officials at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California were hopeful the international project would launch on time despite the rocket's problems.
"The feeling here is that if there is any slip it will be a short one and it will fit within the launch period," laboratory spokeswoman Mary Beth Murrill said.

Cassini is to orbit Saturn, sending back data and pictures for about four years. It will also release a small probe, built by the European Space Agency, to descend into the atmosphere of Saturn's largest moon, also called Titan.
